en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 91, the Brahmāyu Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Videhas with a large Saṅgha of monks, with about five hundred monks.
Now at that time, the brahmin Brahmāyu was residing in Mithilā;
he was aged, elderly, advanced in years, come to the last stage of life, being one hundred and twenty years of age, and had mastered the three Vedas along with their vocabularies and ritual manuals.

He was one who had mastered the Vedas with their vocabularies and ritual exegeses, including the Itihāsas as the fifth; he was a philologist and a grammarian, and he was unskilled in none of the Lokāyata or the marks of a Great Man.
Then the brahmin Brahmāyu heard:
"Friends, the ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from a Sakyan clan, is wandering on tour among the Videhas with a large community of monks, with about five hundred monks."
Furthermore, this excellent report of Master Gotama has spread abroad:

"Indeed, that Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Having realized this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, by his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
It is indeed good to see such Arahants.
Now at that time, the brahmin Brahmāyu had a pupil named Uttara, who was a master of the Three Vedas...
He was one who had mastered the Vedas, including the glossaries (nighaṇḍu) and the ritual manuals (keṭubha), along with phonology and etymology, and the histories as the fifth;
he was a master of the words and a grammarian, and he was well-versed in Lokāyata philosophy and the marks of a Great Man.
Then the brahmin Brahmāyu addressed the young man Uttara:

“Dear Uttara, this ascetic Gotama, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, is wandering on tour among the Videhans together with a great Saṅgha of monks, about five hundred monks in number.
Regarding that venerable Gotama, such a glorious report has spread:
‘Indeed, that Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened... [and so on].”
"It is indeed good to see such Arahants.

"Come then, dear Uttara, go to where the ascetic Gotama is; having approached him, find out whether the reputation that has spread concerning the venerable Gotama is true or not, and whether that venerable Gotama is actually as he is reported to be or not."
“In that way, we shall know that venerable Gotama.
“But how, sir, shall I know that venerable Gotama—whether the report concerning that venerable Gotama has arisen as it truly is, or not as it is;
whether that venerable Gotama is such as he is reported to be, or not such?”
“Dear Uttara, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man have come down to us in our mantras; for a Great Man endowed with these, there are only two possible destinies and no other.

If he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch, righteous, a king of Dharma, conqueror of the four quarters, who has established stability in the land and is possessed of the seven treasures.
These are his seven treasures, namely:”
The wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh.
Moreover, he has more than a thousand sons who are brave, heroic in form, and crushers of enemy armies.
Having conquered this earth bounded by the ocean without punishment or sword, but by righteousness alone, he dwells therein.
"But if he goes forth from the home life into homelessness, he will become an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One who removes the veil from the world.
However, dear Uttara, I am the giver of the mantras,
and you are the receiver of the mantras."

“Yes, sir,” the young brahmin Uttara replied to the brahmin Brahmāyu. Rising from his seat, he paid homage to the brahmin Brahmāyu, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and set out on a wandering tour toward the Blessed One in the Videha country.
Traveling by stages, he approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and friendly conversation, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the young brahmin Uttara examined the Blessed One’s body for the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
The young brahmin Uttara saw the thirty-two marks of a Great Man on the Blessed One’s body, with the exception of two.
Regarding two of these marks of a Great Man, he was doubtful, perplexed, undecided, and lacked conviction.
And [his private parts] are concealed in a sheath, and he has a long tongue.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
"This young brahmin Uttara sees my thirty-two marks of a Great Man, with the exception of two."
"Regarding two of the marks of a Great Man, he is doubtful, perplexed, undecided, and lacks confidence:
namely, the sheathed genitals and the long tongue.
Then the Blessed One performed such a feat of psychic power that the brahmin student Uttara saw the Blessed One’s sheathed genitals.
Then the Blessed One, having extended his tongue, stroked and touched both ear canals; he stroked and touched both nostrils; and he covered the entire surface of his forehead with his tongue.
Then it occurred to the young man Uttara:
"The ascetic Gotama is indeed endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man."
"What if I were to follow the ascetic Gotama? I might see his mode of conduct.
Then the young brahmin Uttara followed the Blessed One for seven months, like a shadow that never departs.
Then, at the end of those seven months, the young brahmin Uttara set out on a wandering tour toward Mithilā in the Videha country.
Wandering on his journey by stages, he approached Mithilā, where the brahmin Brahmāyu was staying.
Having approached, he paid homage to the brahmin Brahmāyu and sat down to one side. As the young man Uttara was sitting there to one side, the brahmin Brahmāyu said this to him:
“Is it true, dear Uttara, that the report concerning the venerable Gotama has arisen exactly as he is, and not otherwise?
And is the venerable Gotama such as that report describes, and not otherwise?
“It is exactly as he is, sir, that the report concerning the venerable Gotama has arisen, and not otherwise.”
That venerable Gotama is exactly like that, not otherwise.
That venerable Gotama is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Furthermore, sir, the venerable Gotama has feet that stand firmly.
This too is a mark of a Great Man belonging to that venerable Gotama.
Furthermore, on the soles of the venerable Gotama’s feet, wheels have appeared with a thousand spokes, complete with rims and hubs,
perfect in every aspect… Moreover, the venerable Gotama has long heels…
Moreover, that venerable Gotama has long fingers...
Moreover, that venerable Gotama has soft and tender hands and feet...
Moreover, that venerable Gotama has webbed hands and feet...
Moreover, that venerable Gotama has high-arched feet...
he has calves like those of an antelope...
and while standing without bending, he can touch and rub both knees with the palms of his hands...
Furthermore, that venerable Gotama has his private parts concealed by a sheath;
furthermore, that venerable Gotama is golden-hued, with skin like refined gold;
furthermore, that venerable Gotama has delicate skin. Because of the delicacy of his skin, dust and dirt do not adhere to his body.
Furthermore, that venerable Gotama has a single hair to each pore; the hairs grow one by one from their follicles...
Furthermore, that venerable Gotama has upward-pointing body hairs; the hairs grow pointing upwards, blue-black in color like collyrium, curled, and turned to the right...
Furthermore, that venerable Gotama has a body straight like that of Brahmā...
Furthermore, that venerable Gotama has a prominent chest;
furthermore, that venerable Gotama has a torso like that of a lion;
furthermore, that venerable Gotama has well-rounded shoulders.
Furthermore, Master Gotama is well-proportioned like a banyan tree: as tall as his body is wide, and as wide as his body is tall...
Moreover, Master Gotama has a symmetrical torso...
Furthermore, Master Gotama possesses the supreme sense of taste.
Moreover, that venerable Gotama has a jaw like a lion’s;
moreover, that venerable Gotama has forty teeth;
moreover, that venerable Gotama has even teeth.
Moreover, that venerable Gotama has teeth without gaps... he has very white teeth... he has a broad tongue...
Moreover, that venerable Gotama has a voice like Brahmā, speaking with the tone of the karavika bird...
Moreover, that venerable Gotama has deep blue eyes...
Moreover, that venerable Gotama has eyelashes like those of a cow.
Furthermore, between his eyebrows, Master Gotama has a tuft of hair that is white, soft like cotton...
Moreover, Master Gotama has a cranial protuberance on his head; this too is a mark of a Great Man belonging to Master Gotama.
Thus, Master, Master Gotama is endowed with these thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
Moreover, as Master Gotama walks, he steps forward first with the right foot.
He lifts his foot neither too far nor too close;
he walks neither too fast nor too slowly.
He does not walk with one hip thrust out against the other, nor does he walk with one ankle thrust against the other.
As he walks, he neither raises his thigh nor lowers it; he neither bends his thigh nor twists it.
Indeed, as the venerable Gotama walks, only his lower body moves, and he does not walk by means of bodily strength.
Moreover, when that venerable Gotama looks, he looks with his entire body;
he does not look upward, nor does he look downward;
he does not walk about glancing here and there, but looks only the distance of a plough’s length; and beyond that, his knowledge and vision are unobstructed.
Thus, when entering among the houses, he does not raise his body, nor does he lower his body; he does not bend his body forward, nor does he lean his body backward.
He turns around from his seat neither too far away nor too close; he does not sit down on the seat by clutching it with his hands, nor does he thrust his body onto the seat.
While sitting among the houses, he does not engage in fidgeting with his hands, nor does he engage in fidgeting with his feet.
He does not sit with one knee placed upon the other; he does not sit with one ankle placed upon the other;
nor does he sit with his hand pressed against his chin.

While sitting within a house, he is not startled, does not tremble, does not shake, and is not agitated. Thus, being unstartled, untrembling, unshaking, and unagitated, his hair stands no longer on end.

And while the venerable Gotama was sitting in the midst of the village, he received the water for his bowl without raising the bowl, nor lowering it; he did not bend the bowl forward, nor turn it sideways.
He received the water for his bowl neither too little nor too much.
Thus, he does not wash his bowl making a *khulukhuluka* sound, nor does he wash it by turning it over;
he does not set the bowl on the ground and wash his hands. When his hands are washed, the bowl is considered washed; when the bowl is washed, his hands are considered washed.
He discards the water from the bowl neither too far nor too near, and he does so without scattering it about.
Thus, when receiving the boiled rice, he does not tilt the bowl upward, nor does he tilt it downward; he does not bend the bowl forward, nor does he bend it backward.
He receives the rice neither too little nor too much.
Furthermore, Master Gotama consumes the sauce merely as sauce; he does not add the sauce to the mouthful of food.
Master Gotama turns the morsel over in his mouth two or three times before swallowing it;
not a single grain of rice enters his body unchewed, nor does any grain of rice remain in his mouth when he brings forth another morsel.
That venerable Gotama consumes food experiencing its taste, yet he does not experience craving for its flavor.
Furthermore, that venerable Gotama consumes food endowed with eight factors:
neither for sport, nor for intoxication, nor for physical beauty, nor for adornment, but solely for the maintenance of this body... [and so forth].

"For the sake of sustenance, for the cessation of affliction, and for support of the holy life: 'Thus I shall eliminate old feelings and not give rise to new feelings, and there will be for me maintenance, blamelessness, and a comfortable dwelling.
Having finished his meal, when receiving water for the bowl, he does not tilt the bowl up, nor does he tilt the bowl down; he does not bend the bowl inward, nor does he bend the bowl outward.
He receives the water for the bowl neither too little nor too much.
He does not wash the bowl making a "khulu-khulu" sound, nor does he wash the bowl by turning it over;
he does not set the bowl on the ground to wash his hands. When his hands are washed, the bowl is washed; when the bowl is washed, his hands are washed.
He discards the water from his bowl neither too far nor too near, and he does not discard it carelessly.
Having finished his meal, he does not set the bowl on the ground neither too far nor too near; he is not indifferent to the bowl, yet he does not guard the bowl for too long.
Having finished his meal, he sits in silence for a moment, and he does not let the time for the expression of appreciation pass by.
Having eaten, he expresses his appreciation; he does not criticize that meal, nor does he long for another meal.
Instead, he instructs, exhorts, inspires, and gladdens that assembly with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened that assembly with a discourse on the Dhamma, he rises from his seat and departs.
Thus he does not walk too fast, nor does he walk too slowly; he does not walk with the desire to relieve himself.
The robe on the body of the venerable Gotama is neither too high nor too low; it is neither clinging to the body nor hanging away from the body;
and the wind does not blow the robe away from the body of the venerable Gotama.
And dust and dirt do not cling to the body of that venerable Gotama.
Having gone to a monastery, he sits down on a prepared seat. Having sat down, he washes his feet;
yet that venerable Gotama does not dwell devoted to the practice of adorning his feet.
Having washed his feet, he sat down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
He neither intended for his own harm, nor for the harm of others, nor for the harm of both;
that venerable Gotama sat reflecting only on what is beneficial for himself, beneficial for others, beneficial for both, and beneficial for the whole world.
Thus, having gone to the monastery, he teaches the Dhamma in the assembly; he does not exalt that assembly, nor does he disparage it;
rather, he instructs, urges, inspires, and gladdens that assembly with talk on the Dhamma.
Furthermore, an eightfold-endowed voice issues from the mouth of Master Gotama:
It is distinct, intelligible, sweet, pleasant to hear, clear, not diffuse, deep, and resonant.
Yet, that venerable Gotama makes himself understood with a voice that reaches exactly the assembly, and his sound does not carry beyond the gathering.

Having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by that venerable Gotama with a discourse on the Dhamma, they rise from their seats and depart while still looking back, as if unwilling to leave him.
"Sir, we saw that venerable Gotama going; we saw him standing; we saw him entering among the houses;
we saw him sitting silently among the houses; we saw him eating among the houses;
we saw him sitting silently after he had finished eating; and we saw him giving his blessing after he had finished eating."
"We saw him going to the monastery; we saw him seated in the monastery, silent;
we saw him teaching the Dhamma to the assembly in the monastery.
Such is Master Gotama, and even more than that."

When this was said, the brahmin Brahmāyu rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, uttered this inspired exclamation three times:
“Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One!
Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One!”
"Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One!
Perhaps we might at some time, on some occasion, meet with Master Gotama; perhaps there might be some exchange of conversation.
Then the Blessed One, wandering by stages through the Videha country, arrived at Mithilā.
There the Blessed One was staying at Mithilā in the Maghadeva Mango Grove.
The brahmin householders of Mithilā heard:
"Friends, the ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, while wandering on tour among the Videhas..."
Accompanied by a great community of monks, numbering about five hundred monks, he arrived at Mithilā and was staying there in the Maghadeva Mango Grove.
Now, this excellent report of the venerable Gotama’s fame had spread abroad:

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: an arahant, perfectly enlightened, endowed with clear knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Having realized this world—with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—by his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and the right phrasing; he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
It is indeed good to see such Arahants.
Then the brahmin householders of Mithilā approached the Blessed One; having approached, they...
Some, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side;
some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and having concluded the polite and courteous conversation, sat down to one side;
some extended their joined palms toward the Blessed One and sat down to one side; and some [sat down] in the presence of the Blessed One.
Having announced their names and clans, some sat down to one side; some sat down to one side in silence.
Then the brahmin Brahmāyu heard: "The ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, has arrived at Mithilā and is staying in Mithilā at the Maghadeva Mango Grove.
Thereupon, the brahmin Brahmāyu approached the Maghadeva Mango Grove together with many disciples.
Then, not far from the mango grove, this thought occurred to the brahmin Brahmāyu:
"It would not be fitting for me to approach the ascetic Gotama to see him without having first been announced.
Then the brahmin Brahmāyu addressed a certain young brahmin student:

“Come, young man, go to where the ascetic Gotama is; having approached him, inquire in my name after the ascetic Gotama’s freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical vigor, strength, and well-being, saying:
‘Master Gotama, the brahmin Brahmāyu inquires after your freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical vigor, strength, and well-being.
And speak thus:”
“Master Gotama, the brahmin Brahmāyu is aged, elderly, advanced in years, come to the last stage of life, having reached one hundred and twenty years from birth;
he has mastered the three Vedas, together with their vocabularies, ritual manuals, phonology, and etymologies, as well as the histories as the fifth;
he is a master of the padapāṭha and grammar, and is unskilled in none of the Lokāyata or the marks of a Great Man.”
To whatever extent, sirs, there are brahmin householders living in Mithilā, the brahmin Brahmāyu is declared their foremost—
in terms of wealth—
and the brahmin Brahmāyu is declared their foremost.
Among those who are experts in mantras,
the brahmin Brahmayu is declared to be the foremost—
in both lifespan and fame.
“Thus, sir, I wish to see Master Gotama.
“Very well, sir,” that young brahmin replied to the brahmin Brahmāyu, and he approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and friendly conversation, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, that young brahmin said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, the brahmin Brahmāyu asks after your health, freedom from affliction, physical ease, strength, and well-being;
and he says this:
‘Master Gotama, the brahmin Brahmāyu is aged, elderly, advanced in years, come to the last stage of life, being one hundred and twenty years old.’”
He was well-born and a master of the three Vedas, including the glossaries (nighaṇḍu) and liturgical formulas (keṭubha), the phonology and etymology, and the histories as the fifth;
he was a scholar of the words and a grammarian, unerring in the Lokāyata system and in the marks of a Great Man.
Indeed, among all the brahmins and householders living in Mithilā, Master Brahmāyu is declared to be the foremost.
Among those who possess wealth,
the Brahmin is declared the foremost; among those who possess mantras, the Brahmin is declared the foremost.
“Brahmāyu the brahmin is declared to be the foremost among them in terms of both lifespan and fame.
He wishes to see you, Master Gotama.”
“When it pleases you, young man, the brahmin Brahmāyu may depart.
Then that young man approached the brahmin Brahmāyu; having approached him, he said this to the brahmin Brahmāyu:
“I have been granted leave by the ascetic Gotama.”
"Now, venerable sir, please do as you think fit.
Then the brahmin Brahmāyu approached the Blessed One.
The assembly saw the brahmin Brahmāyu coming from afar.
Having seen him, he made room for him as one would for a well-known and renowned person.
Then the brahmin Brahmāyu said this to that assembly:
"Enough, sirs."
“Sit down on your own seats;
I shall sit here in the presence of the ascetic Gotama.
Then the brahmin Brahmāyu approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the brahmin Brahmāyu examined the Blessed One’s body for the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
The brahmin Brahmāyu saw the thirty-two marks of a Great Man on the Blessed One’s body, with the exception of two.
He was doubtful, perplexed, undecided, and lacked confidence regarding two of the marks of a Great Man:
the male organ being sheathed and the tongue being large.
Then the brahmin Brahmāyu addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“I have heard that there are thirty-two marks of a Great Man;
of these, I do not see two.”
In your body, O Gotama,
is your private organ concealed by a sheath, as is the case with the best of men?
Is your tongue not like that of a woman?
Are you one whose tongue is abundant?
So that we may understand it as it is,
please incline this abundant [teaching] and dispel our doubt, O Seer.
For the sake of benefit in this present life and for happiness in the future,
we ask you, having been granted the opportunity.
"Whatever has been aspired for.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
"This Brahmin Brahmāyu sees my thirty-two marks of a Great Man, with the exception of two."
“He has doubt, uncertainty, lack of resolve, and lack of confidence regarding two of the marks of a Great Man:
the male organ being sheathed and the long tongue.
Then the Blessed One performed such a feat of psychic power that the brahmin Brahmayu saw the Blessed One’s male organ was sheathed.
Then the Blessed One, having extended his tongue, touched and stroked both ear-holes; he touched and stroked both nostrils; and he completely covered the circle of his forehead with his tongue.
Then the Blessed One replied to the brahmin Brahmāyu in verses:
“Those thirty-two marks that you have heard of...”
All these marks of a Great Man are upon my body;
let there be no doubt in you, O Brahmin.
What is to be directly known has been directly known,
what is to be developed has been developed;
what is to be abandoned has been abandoned by me.
Therefore, O Brahmin, I am a Buddha—
for the sake of welfare in this very life and for happiness in the life to come.
"Having been granted leave, ask whatever you desire. Then,
this thought occurred to the brahmin Brahmāyu:
“I have been granted an opportunity by the ascetic Gotama.
What then should I ask the ascetic Gotama:
‘Concerning matters pertaining to the present life, or concerning matters pertaining to the future life?’”
Then it occurred to the brahmin Brahmāyu:
"I am indeed skilled in matters pertaining to this present life.
Others also ask me about matters pertaining to this present life."
“What if I were now to ask the ascetic Gotama about matters pertaining to the life hereafter?
Then the brahmin Brahmāyu addressed the Blessed One in verses:
“How does one become a brahmin? How does one become a true priest?”
How does one become a master of knowledge?
How, O sir, does one become a knower of the three Vedas?
And how is one called a "Sotthiya"?
How, sir, does one become an Arahant?
How does one become a Kevalin?
And how, sir, does one become a Muni?
“How is one called a Buddha?
Then the Blessed One replied to the brahmin Brahmāyu in verse:
“He who knows his former abodes, …”
He sees both heaven and the states of woe;
having reached the destruction of birth,
the sage has perfected his direct knowledge.
He knows the mind to be purified,
entirely liberated from lusts;
he has abandoned birth and death.
Perfect in the holy life,
having reached the further shore of all phenomena,
such a one is called a Buddha.
When this was said, the brahmin Brahmāyu rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder,
prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, kissed the Blessed One’s feet, stroked them with his hands, and announced his name:
“I am the brahmin Brahmāyu, Master Gotama.”
“Master Gotama, I am a brahmin named Brahmāyu.
Then that assembly was struck with a sense of wonder and amazement, thinking:
“How extraordinary, indeed! How marvelous, indeed!”
"For indeed, this brahmin Brahmāyu, who is well-known and renowned, would perform such a supreme act of self-surrender.
Then the Blessed One said this to the brahmin Brahmāyu:
"Enough, brahmin! Arise; sit down on your own seat, since your mind has gained confidence in me."
Then the brahmin Brahmāyu rose and sat down on his own seat.
Then the Blessed One gave the brahmin Brahmāyu a progressive discourse, namely:
a talk on generosity, a talk on virtuous conduct, and a talk on heaven.
He proclaimed the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit in renunciation.

When the Blessed One knew that the brahmin Brahmāyu’s mind was ready, pliable, free from hindrances, uplifted, and confident, he then set forth that Dhamma teaching which is uniquely proclaimed by Buddhas:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Just as a clean cloth, free from dark stains, would properly take up dye, even so,
while sitting right there on that very seat, the dustless, stainless eye of Dhamma arose in the brahmin Brahmāyu:
"Whatever is subject to origination, all that is subject to cessation."

Then the brahmin Brahmāyu, having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and plunged into the Dhamma—having crossed over doubt, being free from perplexity, having attained self-confidence, and becoming independent of others in the Teacher’s instruction—said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!”
"Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden,
or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
just so has the Dhamma been made clear by Master Gotama in many ways."
“I go for refuge to Master Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
And may Master Gotama, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, consent to accept a meal from me tomorrow.”
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then the brahmin Brahmāyu, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Then, at the end of that night, the brahmin Brahmāyu had various kinds of excellent hard and soft food prepared in his own residence and had the time announced to the Blessed One:
“It is time, Master Gotama; the meal is ready.
Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, went to the residence of the brahmin Brahmāyu and sat down on the prepared seat together with the community of monks.
Then the brahmin Brahmāyu, with his own hands, personally served and satisfied the community of monks headed by the Buddha for seven days with excellent hard and soft foods.
Then, at the end of those seven days, the Blessed One set out on a wandering tour among the Videhas.
Not long after the Blessed One had departed, the brahmin Brahmāyu passed away.

Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting there to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the brahmin Brahmāyu has passed away.
What is his destination, what is his future state?
“Bhikkhus, the brahmin Brahmāyu was wise; he practiced in accordance with the Dhamma and did not trouble me on account of the Dhamma.”

“Bhikkhus, with the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, the brahmin Brahmāyu is of spontaneous birth (*opapātiko*), attaining final Nibbāna there, no longer subject to return from that world.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Elated, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Brahmāyusutta is finished; this is the first.
